title: The Quran affirms the Bible of Muhammad's day
claim: The Quran treats the Torah and Gospel of Muhammad's own day as real, present and authoritative. It 'confirms what came before it' (Quran 3:3). It asks why Jews come to Muhammad for judgment 'while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah' (5:43) — with them, in the present tense. It commands 'the People of the Gospel' to 'judge by what Allah has revealed therein' (5:46-47). It tells Jews and Christians they are 'on nothing' until they uphold the Torah and Gospel (5:68). It tells Muhammad himself, if in doubt, to 'ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you' (10:94). And it declares that 'none can alter His words' (6:115; 18:27). A corrupted, unreliable Bible cannot be what any of those verses mean. So the tahrif, or corruption, doctrine faces a fork. Corruption before Muhammad contradicts the Quran. Corruption after Muhammad is ruled out by surviving manuscripts.

A second line argues that the Injil is a distinct revelation given to Jesus, not the four Gospels Christians possess. On this account affirmation and corruption sit together: the Quran affirms what is genuinely from Allah in their books, and corrects the rest.

Quran 5:47 commands present-tense judgment by the Gospel. Quran 10:94 makes readers of the earlier Scripture the check on Muhammad's own revelation. None of that is coherent if those texts were unreliable. The 'lost original Injil' answer posits a book with no historical or manuscript existence at all, and 5:47 addresses the actual People of the Gospel and what they hold. Neither horn is escaped. The answers move the problem rather than resolve it.

plain.d: Most Muslims believe the Bible was changed. That is why they will not accept it as evidence. So every other argument stalls right here. This case answers it from the Quran itself, not from ours.

Now read the verses again. Quran 5:43 says the Torah with them holds Allah's judgment now. Quran 5:47 tells Christians to judge by the Gospel now. Quran 10:94 makes those same readers the check on Muhammad's message. None of that works if the books could not be trusted.

Strong for you. No Muslim scholar has published a clean answer. The replies move the problem instead of solving it. Corruption before Muhammad contradicts the Quran. Corruption after him is closed off by manuscripts, which is the next case.

title: Early Islam blamed twisted meaning, not a changed text
claim: The charge that the Bible's text was falsified — tahrif al-nass — is not the Quran's teaching, and it was not early Islam's. Gordon Nickel studied the earliest Quran commentaries, including Muqatil ibn Sulayman in the 8th century and al-Tabari, who died in 923. They understood the tampering verses as misinterpretation, concealment and mispronunciation by Jews and Christians. That is tahrif al-mana, corruption of meaning, not of text. Ibn Abbas, cited in Sahih al-Bukhari's Book of Tawhid, said no one can remove the words of Allah from His books; people distort meanings by misreading. The full text-corruption doctrine only crystallised with Ibn Hazm of Cordoba, who died in 1064 — four centuries after Muhammad. It hardened as a polemical necessity once the differences between Bible and Quran were pressed.

response: Muslim apologists reply that tahrif al-nass is no medieval invention. The Quran says 'a party of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort it' (2:75). It condemns 'those who write the Book with their own hands, then say: this is from Allah' (2:79) — physical writing, not mere misreading. They also note that the same Ibn Abbas, in Sahih al-Bukhari 7363, says the People of the Book 'changed and altered' their Book and wrote it with their own hands. So the early testimony cuts both ways. On this view Ibn Hazm systematised the doctrine rather than inventing it. Islamweb argues the same in its fatwa on judging by the Torah and Gospel.

rationale: The load-bearing facts are conceded inside Islamic sources and in academic scholarship. The earliest exegetes overwhelmingly read the tampering verses as distortion of meaning. Bukhari preserves Ibn Abbas denying that anyone can change Allah's words in His books. Even reviewers sympathetic to Islam grant that only Ibn Hazm and al-Maqdisi held thoroughgoing textual corruption among the classical authorities. Quran 2:79 addresses a party writing false material and selling it. It never says the Torah's manuscript tradition was rewritten, and no early source identifies when, where or by whom that global rewrite happened. The doctrine every dawah presentation depends on is historically late.

Ibn Hazm, they say, organised the doctrine rather than invented it.

title: The Bible of 600 AD is the Bible today
claim: Whatever text the Quran affirmed in Muhammad's day, between 610 and 632 AD, is recoverable — and it is the same in substance as today's Bible. The Dead Sea Scrolls date from about 250 BC to 70 AD. They include the complete Great Isaiah Scroll, from about 125 BC, with Isaiah 53 intact, and they substantially match the Masoretic text behind modern Old Testaments. The Septuagint translation dates to the 3rd and 2nd centuries BC. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, from the mid-4th century AD, each contain the complete New Testament or nearly so, and they are the base of modern critical editions. They predate Muhammad by about 250 years. So the second horn is sealed: no corruption after Muhammad is possible, because the text from before him survives, and it is our text.

The originals of Moses and Jesus were lost or altered in the centuries before Qumran and Sinaiticus. So today's Bible faithfully transmits a text that had already gone wrong. IslamQA adds two supports. The Dead Sea Scrolls themselves show textual plurality, with variant editions of Jeremiah and Samuel. And the New Testament critical apparatus records hundreds of thousands of variants. That proves the transmission was human and fallible, not divinely guarded as the Quran's is claimed to be.

If the Bible was already corrupt centuries before Muhammad, then the Quran's commands to judge by it, its claim that the Torah 'with them' contains Allah's judgment, and its instruction to resolve doubt by asking its readers are all commendations of a corrupt book. The variant-plurality point is a category error. No Dead Sea Scroll and no New Testament variant tradition removes the crucifixion, the resurrection or divine sonship — the things the Quran needs absent. Those are textually secure across every manuscript stream. The manuscripts leave no window in which the required wholesale corruption could have happened.

plain.d: If the Bible was changed, it happened at some point in time. Manuscripts let us check when. Muhammad received the Quran between 610 and 632 AD. So the question is simple. What did the Bible look like before then?

The Dead Sea Scrolls were copied between about 250 BC and 70 AD. They include the complete Great Isaiah Scroll, from about 125 BC, with Isaiah 53 intact. The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, is older still — the 3rd to 2nd century BC. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus date to the mid-300s AD. Each holds the whole New Testament, or nearly all of it.

These copies predate Muhammad by 250 to 900 years. They are the base of the modern critical editions. So the Bible read in 600 AD is in substance the Bible read today. There is no window left for a later rewrite.

IslamQA grants the manuscripts and moves the date. The corruption, they say, is older than any of these copies. The books of Moses and Jesus were altered long before Qumran or Sinaiticus. They add two things. The Scrolls show variety, with different editions of Jeremiah and Samuel. And the New Testament has hundreds of thousands of variants.

Strong for you, because the reply falls into the first trap. If the Bible was already corrupt, the Quran told people to judge by a corrupt book. And no variant in any manuscript removes the crucifixion, the resurrection or the divine Son. Those are secure across every copy we have.

title: Quran 4:157 denies the crucifixion that historians confirm
claim: Quran 4:157 says of the Jews: 'they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but another was made to resemble him to them.' That is a single verse, composed about 600 years after the event and more than a thousand kilometres away. All four gospels report the event. So does a pre-Pauline creed dated to within a few years of it (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). So do two non-Christian historians: Josephus (Antiquities 18.3.3) and Tacitus (Annals 15.44). Critical historians across the spectrum treat it as bedrock. Bart Ehrman, an agnostic, writes: 'One of the most certain facts of history is that Jesus was crucified on orders of the Roman prefect of Judea, Pontius Pilate.' Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist, writes: 'The fact of the death of Jesus as a consequence of crucifixion is indisputable.' No case for the denial rests on historical method. It rests only on the Quran's authority.

And a minority scholarly stream, documented by Todd Lawson and argued by Mahmoud Ayoub, reads 4:157 as denying only the Jews' boast of agency: they did not kill him, God's plan prevailed. On that reading the event itself is left neither affirmed nor denied.

title: Virgin-born, sinless, raised alive: the Quran's Jesus
claim: The Quran gives Jesus a profile it gives no one else, including Muhammad. He is virgin-born (3:47). He is 'the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter' (3:45). He is announced as 'a pure boy', that is, sinless (19:19). He works miracles, healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead (3:49; 5:110). He never dies; 'Allah raised him to Himself', so he is alive in heaven now (4:158). In Islamic eschatology he returns at the end of the age (Sahih al-Bukhari 3448). Muhammad, by contrast, is commanded to 'ask forgiveness for your sin' (47:19; 48:2), performs no miracle in the Quran, and is dead in Medina. Every data point the Quran itself supplies points to Jesus's uniqueness — and then forbids the conclusion they suggest.

response: The Quran heads off the inference itself: 'The example of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him: Be, and he was' (3:59). A fatherless origin proves creative sovereignty, not divinity — otherwise Adam, who had no father and no mother, would be more divine still. Omar Suleiman of the Yaqeen Institute develops this reading. Every miracle in 3:49 carries the refrain bi-idhnillah, 'by Allah's permission', marking Jesus as an empowered servant rather than a source. His sinlessness and his ascension are honours Allah bestows on whom He wills, and prophets differ in gifts (2:253) without differing in nature. Jesus's greatness is affirmed exactly as the second greatest of servants — never as God's son, a title he himself will disown (5:116-117).

rationale: The Adam analogy and the bi-idhnillah refrain are genuine, coherent answers to the virgin birth and the miracles taken one at a time. This is Islam's best-drilled ground. But the analogy covers origin only. Adam sinned. Jesus is the only figure the Quran calls pure. He is never shown sinning, never recorded dying, and is titled al-Masih without that title ever being defined. He is stationed alive in heaven pending his return — while the Quran's final prophet is twice told to seek forgiveness for his sin. The cumulative asymmetry is unanswered as a whole, even though every part has a rehearsed reply. That is why this is contested rather than unrefuted, and a door-opener rather than a defeater.

Quran 5:47 commands: 'Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein', with a warning that whoever does not judge by it is 'defiantly disobedient'. Now run the test. The Gospel possessed by every People of the Gospel community in 632 AD was the fourfold Gospel, its text secured by Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus two centuries earlier. title: Uthman's order to burn the other Qurans
claim: The contrast between a perfectly preserved Quran and a corrupted Bible fails on Islam's own sources. Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 records that within about twenty years of Muhammad's death Muslims were 'differing about the Quran as the Jews and Christians differed about their Scripture'. So Caliph Uthman had one recension copied and ordered all other Quranic material, 'whether written in fragmentary manuscripts or whole copies, be burnt'. Companion codices differed. Early Islamic sources report that Ibn Masud's codex lacked Surahs 1, 113 and 114, and Bukhari 4977 preserves the dispute, while Ubayy ibn Ka'b's contained two extra surahs. Bukhari 4992 shows companions disputing recitations in Muhammad's own lifetime, resolved by the 'seven ahruf' concession. A text preserved by destroying its variant witnesses cannot indict the Bible for having variant witnesses that survived.

title: God who loves, or God who is love
claim: 1 John 4:8 makes love God's essence: 'God is love'. Love is inherently other-directed — lover, beloved, love. The Trinity grounds that eternally, since the Father loves the Son 'before the foundation of the world' (John 17:24). A unitarian monad, by contrast, had no one to love before creation. So either love is not essential to Allah, and he became loving when he made creatures, or he was eternally self-focused. There is a corollary. 'Father' is not among the 99 names, and Allah is never called Father in the Quran. Love in the Quran is predominantly conditional — 'Allah loves those who...' and 'Allah loves not the transgressors' (2:190; 3:31-32) — while 5:18 rebukes Jews and Christians for calling themselves children of Allah.

First, al-Wadud, 'the Most Loving', appears twice (11:90; 85:14), so divine love is a real Quranic attribute, and Sahih Muslim 2751a says His mercy prevails over His wrath; the claim that Islam's God lacks love is simply false. Second, Abdullah al Andalusi's rebuttal to William Lane Craig: an attribute can be eternal as a disposition without being eternally exercised. Allah is eternally al-Khaliq, Creator, without an eternal creation, so likewise eternally loving without an eternal beloved. Demanding eternal actualisation proves too much, since it would require an eternal object of mercy and wrath as well. Third, Bassam Zawadi and al Andalusi argue that Craig's definition of perfect love as self-giving to another person begs the question in favour of Trinitarianism.

But the disposition-versus-actualisation distinction is a serious answer that Craig's argument must work to defeat. The honest grade splits the claim. The comparative textual point holds: the Bible makes love essential and eternally actual in a way the Quran does not. The philosophical point, that a monad cannot be perfectly loving, is contested.

plain.d: 1 John 4:8 says God is love. Not only that He loves. Love is His nature. But love needs someone to love. The Trinity grounds that: the Father loved the Son "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24).

title: The clay birds come from a 2nd-century legend
claim: The Quran's two signature Jesus miracles are absent from the canonical gospels, and both have documented literary ancestors in Christian apocrypha. The child Jesus forming birds from clay and breathing life into them (3:49; 5:110) parallels the Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2:1-5, a Greek text of the mid-2nd century — a legend cycle in which the boy Jesus also strikes playmates dead. Jesus speaking from the cradle (19:29-33; 3:46) parallels the Arabic Infancy Gospel, a Syriac-derived compilation of the 5th or 6th century, where the infant says 'I am the Son of God'. Both texts predate the Quran by centuries and circulated in Syriac and Arabic Christian settings. So the Quran presents legendary material composed 100 to 500 years after Jesus as historical revelation. That is exactly what a 7th-century author absorbing local Christian folklore would produce.

title: What Jesus meant by 'Son of God'
claim: The Quran attacks a 'Son of God' its opponents never held, meaning physical offspring, while the actual biblical claim goes unaddressed. 'Son of God' is a royal and divine title (Psalm 2:7), and in Jesus's usage it asserted equality with God. John 5:18 says the Jews sought to kill him because 'he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God'. Consider his own claims. 'Before Abraham was, I am' (John 8:58), met with an attempted stoning. Mark 14:61-64: 'I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven' — the language of Daniel 7 — ruled capital blasphemy. John 20:28: Thomas says 'My Lord and my God', and is blessed, not rebuked. Every one of these texts exists in manuscripts predating Islam by 200 to 450 years — P66 and P75 from about 200 AD, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus from the 4th century. Whatever one thinks of their truth, the claims demonstrably predate the Quran's denial of them.

response: The strongest reply, argued by Shabir Ally and Bassam Zawadi, has five parts. Second, John 8:58's ego eimi is not the divine name: the Greek Exodus 3:14 renders the name as ho on, and the healed blind man says ego eimi in John 9:9. Third, the strongest claims cluster in John, the latest gospel, reflecting developed church theology — the Synoptic Jesus prays, calls the Father 'the only true God' (John 17:3), and disclaims omniscience (Mark 13:32). Fourth, Mark 14:62's exaltation claim is one a Jewish agent of God could make, and blasphemy verdicts were elastic. Fifth, Jesus never says 'I am God; worship me.'

title: Confirming the Bible, the Quran never quotes it
claim: The Quran claims to confirm, musaddiq, the Torah and Gospel (2:97; 3:3; 5:48; 46:12). Yet in 6,236 verses it contains essentially no verbatim quotation of the texts it confirms. The single near-exception is 21:105: 'We wrote in the Zabur... My righteous servants shall inherit the earth', which corresponds to Psalm 37:29. Its biblical narratives arrive garbled through midrash and apocrypha — Cain's raven from Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer (5:31), Abraham in the fiery furnace from midrash (21:68-69), Mary confused with Miriam sister of Aaron (19:28). Contrast the New Testament, which quotes the Old Testament about 300 times, explicitly. That is what confirming previous scripture looks like. Sidney Griffith's scholarship confirms that no written Arabic Bible existed before Islam. The Quran's biblical knowledge is oral and homiletic, which fits Muhammad's documented contacts — Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Khadija's Christian cousin, who 'used to write the Gospel in Arabic' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3) — and the accusation recorded in 25:4-5.

title: The Injil: a gospel nobody has ever seen
claim: The Quran speaks of 'the Injil' as a single book Allah gave to Jesus (5:46; 57:27), which mainstream Islam says was later lost or corrupted, leaving the four gospels as unreliable human residue. There are two problems. First, no trace of any such book exists — no manuscript, no fragment, no citation by any ancient author, friend or enemy, in the seven centuries between Jesus and Muhammad. From the earliest records 'gospel', euangelion, was the proclamation about Jesus, and the written gospels are biographies about him. That is a category the Quran appears to misunderstand. Second, the Quran forecloses the lost-book escape itself. Quran 5:47 commands 'let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it' — a present-tense command in 610 to 632 AD, presupposing an Injil then in Christian hands. Demonstrably that was the four gospels, complete in 4th-century codices. Either those gospels were trustworthy, and Islam's Christology is falsified by them, or they were corrupt, and Allah commanded people to judge by a corrupted book he was simultaneously confirming.

Quran 5:47 then commands Christians to judge by what remains of the genuine revelation inside their books. The absence of a separate manuscript is expected, since it was lost early, and that is the whole reason the Quran was sent. The revisionist line, argued by V. A. Mohamad Ashrof and other modernists, concedes that the lost-book thesis is a myth. On that view the Quran's Injil simply is the gospel possessed by 7th-century Christians, treated as containing genuine revelation. The corruption verses then target misinterpretation and concealment rather than textual loss. Gordon Nickel's work on the early tafsir supports that reading.

title: A sun setting in a muddy spring (18:86)
claim: Quran 18:86 says Dhul-Qarnayn travelled until 'he reached the setting-place of the sun; he found it setting in a muddy spring'. The parallel at 18:90 gives a literal rising-place, where the sun rises on a people with no shelter from it. Early tafsir shows this was understood literally. Al-Tabari preserves narrations taking the sun as actually setting in the spring, and Ibn Kathir describes 'a blackened, muddy and stinking spring'. A supporting hadith exists in Sunan Abi Dawud 4002: 'It sets in a spring of warm water.' Albani graded its chain sahih, though some scholars argue the 'spring' wording is the narrator's description rather than the Prophet's. Either way, the tafsir record independently evidences a literal cosmology.

sources.name: Sunan Abi Dawud 4002 (Albani: sahih chain; wording disputed)

response: IslamQA 176375 answers that the verse describes what Dhul-Qarnayn perceived from his vantage point. 'He found it' means it appeared to him, just as English speakers say 'sunset' without meaning the sun moves. He simply reached the westernmost point of his journey, a shoreline where the sun appeared to sink into dark water. That is phenomenological language, not cosmology. The Abu Dawud hadith's wording is disputed, since some hold the 'spring' phrase belongs to the narrator and not the Prophet, so it cannot establish doctrine. The authentic description, they add, is that the sun 'prostrates beneath the Throne' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3199) — a metaphysical statement rather than a physical one.

responseSource.name: IslamQA 176375

rationale: The Arabic can grammatically bear a phenomenological reading, and the supporting hadith's import is disputed, so this is not admitted. But the phenomenological defence is anachronistic. The parallel rising-place at 18:90, the mirrored structure of the journey, and the earliest tafsir record all show that the first Muslim generations read it as real cosmology, consistent with late-antique Near Eastern belief. The defence requires the earliest interpreters to have misread their own book.

title: Quran 86:7 and 23:14 repeat Greek medicine
claim: Quran 86:5-7 says man is created from 'a gushing fluid, proceeding from between the backbone and the ribs'. Semen is produced in the testes, not the torso. The verse echoes the Greek view that semen descends from the region of the back, and classical tafsir took it anatomically. Separately, Quran 23:14 gives the embryonic sequence: drop, then clinging clot, then chewed lump, then bones, then bones clothed with flesh. That tracks Galen's four stages, including Galen's error — bone forming first and then being clothed with flesh, whereas muscle and bone develop concurrently. Medieval Arabic medicine itself mapped the Quranic terms onto Galen's stages. And the embryo is never a 'clot of blood'.

sources.name: WikiIslam — Embryology in the Quran
Answering Islam — 'Alaqa and other embryological stages
IslamQA 118879 — commentary on 86:6-7

response: IslamQA 118879, Maurice Bucaille and the iERA embryology paper answer both passages. On 86:5-7, sulb and tara'ib may be a merism for the whole torso, or may refer to the man's loins and the woman's chest, meaning the fluid of both parents. Some modern writers argue the terms denote the embryological origin-sites of the gonads, which do form near the kidneys before descending. On 23:14, the stages are broad visual descriptions accessible to a 7th-century audience. Alaqah means 'clinging thing', which is accurate for implantation, and 'then' need not be strictly sequential. Keith Moore endorsed the compatibility of these terms with modern embryology.

responseSource.name: IslamQA 118879; Bucaille; iERA embryology paper (later revised)

rationale: The reinterpretations are post hoc. Classical exegetes read 86:7 anatomically, and no reading rescues fluid physically gushing from between backbone and ribs. On embryology, the sequence matches Galen down to sharing Galen's specific bones-then-flesh error, and Muslim physicians for centuries used the Quranic terms as translations of Galen's stages. Keith Moore's endorsement came in a Saudi-sponsored context and is not accepted by the scientific community, and the iERA paper was withdrawn and revised after criticism. A 'broad visual description' that reproduces the precise erroneous schema of the era's dominant Greek medicine is evidence of human sourcing.

title: Mary, sister of Aaron — 1,400 years apart
claim: The Quran calls Mary the mother of Jesus 'sister of Aaron' (19:28), calls her mother 'the wife of Imran' (3:35), and calls Mary 'daughter of Imran' (66:12). That is exactly the family of Miriam in the Bible: Miriam, daughter of Amram, which is Imran, and sister of Aaron and Moses (Exodus 15:20; Numbers 26:59). She lived about 1,400 years before Mary. The triple match — father Imran, brother Aaron, and the identical name Maryam and Miriam — indicates the two women were conflated. Crucially, this objection is as old as Islam. In Sahih Muslim 2135, the Christians of Najran put precisely this problem to Mughira ibn Shu'ba, and Muhammad's answer was that people 'used to give names after the names of Apostles and pious persons before them'.

sources.name: Sahih Muslim 2135
Answering Islam — Is Mary the Sister of Aaron?
Abu Amina Elias — Why Mary is called sister of Aaron

response: The Prophet himself answered this in Sahih Muslim 2135, and Abu Amina Elias develops the answer. Semitic naming convention attached people to revered ancestors. 'Sister of Aaron' means a woman of the Aaronic or priestly line — compare Luke 1:5, which calls Elizabeth one 'of the daughters of Aaron', and Mary was her kinswoman. 'Daughter of Imran' likewise denotes descent from the house of Imran, or Amram, and Surah 3 is named 'the Family of Imran', which signals lineage language. So there is no confusion here, only idiom.

responseSource.name: Sahih Muslim 2135 (Muhammad's own recorded answer); Abu Amina Elias

rationale: The steelman is real, since Luke 1:5 shows that tribal-descent idiom exists. But it does not cover the evidence. The Quran never uses 'sister of X' as a lineage idiom anywhere else. It does not merely link Mary to Aaron; it gives her the full Exodus family — father Imran, brother Aaron, and the identical name. And 3:35-36 narrates Imran's wife giving birth to Mary as one continuous story. A lineage idiom explains one datum, not three converging ones. That the difficulty was spotted by 7th-century Christians, and required a recorded answer, confirms that the natural reading was and is the problem.

title: The golden calf, made by 'the Samaritan' (20:85)
claim: Quran 20:85-97 says the golden calf at Sinai was made not by Aaron, as in Exodus 32, but by 'al-Samiri' — the Samaritan. The Samaritans as a people emerged after the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom, from 722 BC at the earliest, roughly seven centuries after the Exodus period. Scholars note the story likely reflects later anti-Samaritan polemic, since Samaritans were associated with calf-worship at Bethel and Dan, retrojected into the Exodus narrative. The Quran also transfers blame away from Aaron, whom the Bible explicitly names as the calf's maker.

sources.name: Answering Islam — Samaritans in the time of Moses?
Islamic Awareness — The 'Samaritan' Error In The Qur'an?
Answering Islam — response to Islamic Awareness

response: Islamic Awareness argues that 'al-Samiri' is an attributive name for one individual, not necessarily 'the Samaritan'. It could derive from a clan or place name; 1 Kings 16:24 shows 'Shemer' as a personal name predating the city of Samaria. Alternatively, Samaritan tradition itself claims pre-exilic Israelite origins, so the name's referent may be older than critics allow. And the Quran corrects rather than copies the biblical account, by clearing a prophet, Aaron, of idol-making.

responseSource.name: Islamic Awareness — 'The Samaritan Error In The Quran?'

rationale: The etymological escape route is linguistically possible. 'Al-Samiri' need not be an ethnonym, and 'Shemer' as a name is attested early. But it is special pleading against the most natural Arabic reading, in which al-Samiri is exactly the ethnic term as classical usage renders it, and the narrative fits known post-biblical polemical motifs. Neither side can strictly prove the referent, though the critic's reading is the more probable one. And the exoneration of Aaron against Exodus 32 remains a separate, unanswered divergence.

plain.t: Why the name is a problem
plain.d: The Samaritans came from the region of Samaria. That region was named long after the Exodus. Its people were resettled after the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC. That is about seven centuries too late. Scholars think the story reflects later feeling against Samaritans, who were linked with calf-worship at Bethel and Dan.

title: Dhul-Qarnayn matches a Christian Alexander legend
claim: The Quran tells of Dhul-Qarnayn, the Two-Horned One. He journeys to the setting-place and the rising-place of the sun. He builds a wall of iron and brass that imprisons Gog and Magog until the end times. That story closely parallels the Syriac Alexander Legend. It is a Christian propaganda text. Its final form dates to about 629-630 AD, with a 6th-century core. Kevin van Bladel published on this in 2008. Tommaso Tesei followed in 2023, with Oxford University Press. Both argue that the Quranic account depends on the legend. The sequence is the same. So is the two-horned motif, since Alexander is horned on his coins. So is the fetid water at the sunset place, and so is the wall. A Greek pagan king, remembered through Christian legend, appears in the Quran as a monotheist hero. And the geography belongs to legend, not to history.

Cyrus was friendly to monotheists, and he is the two-horned ram of Daniel 8:20. Others say he is an unknown ancient king. On chronology, the Syriac Legend reached its final form about 629-630 AD. That may be too late to be a source for a Meccan surah. So both may draw on a common older oral tradition. On theology, the Quran retells a story its audience already knew. The questions came through Jews, and the Quran corrects the story toward monotheism. A shared narrative frame is not an error. And the Quran omits the legend's explicitly Christian elements.

Classical exegetes themselves commonly identified Dhul-Qarnayn with Alexander. Even the common-source concession still grants the decisive point. The Quran presents legendary material as factual history — a literal setting-place of the sun, and an eschatological wall no one has found.

title: Seven heavens and stars as missiles (67:5)
claim: The Quran describes the sky as a solid structure: a ceiling held up without visible pillars (13:2; 31:10), which could fall on people in pieces (34:9), with seven stacked heavens (67:3). The lowest is adorned with 'lamps', that is stars, which Allah made 'missiles against the devils' (67:5; compare 37:6-10). Quran 72:8-9 has jinn who ascend to eavesdrop pelted with burning flames. This treats stars and meteors as the same class of object. Meteors are dust grains burning in the atmosphere; stars are distant suns. Mainstream tafsir confirms the reading. Qatada, quoted in Ibn Kathir on 67:5, says: 'These stars were only created for three purposes: adornment for the heaven, missiles for the devils, and signs for navigation.'

sources.name: Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 67:5
WikiIslam — Shooting Stars in the Quran

response: Ibn Kathir on 67:5, and IslamQA treatments, answer that in Arabic najm and kawkab can denote any luminous heavenly body, including meteors. So 67:5 speaks of luminous projectiles from the lower heaven, not literal suns being thrown. Ibn Kathir himself explains that 'a meteor of fire detaches itself from the star', with the star remaining in place. The seven heavens are unseen metaphysical realms, not physical shells, and canopy language is protective metaphor, since the atmosphere genuinely does shield the earth. These verses describe the unseen, which is a theological datum and not falsifiable by astronomy.

Ibn Kathir's detaching-meteor gloss is itself an attempted harmonisation, and it still ties meteors physically to stars, which is false. The reading fits precisely the 7th-century phenomenology of shooting stars. The metaphysical-realms defence is viable in isolation, but the missile verses anchor the cosmology to visible objects.

title: Abrogation (2:106) and the satanic verses reports
claim: Quran 2:106 and 16:101 state that Allah replaces some revealed verses with others. Critics ask why an omniscient God's eternal speech needs cancelling and reissuing within 23 years, and 16:101 records that contemporaries concluded 'You are but a forger.' The sharpest test case is the satanic-verses incident. Early Islamic sources — al-Tabari, Ibn Sa'd and al-Waqidi — record that Muhammad, wishing for reconciliation with the Quraysh, recited praise of the goddesses al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat after 53:19-20: 'these are the exalted cranes whose intercession is hoped for'. The words were later attributed to Satan and cancelled. Early exegetes read 22:52 — 'Satan threw something into the recitation of every prophet' — as the divine comment on the event. Shahab Ahmed of Harvard, in 'Before Orthodoxy', showed that the incident was a standard element of Muslim historical memory for Islam's first 150 years or so, and only later became universally rejected.

sources.name: Shahab Ahmed — Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam (Harvard UP)
Answering Islam — The Story of the Cranes
SeekersGuidance — What Is Abrogation (Naskh)?

response: On abrogation, SeekersGuidance answers that naskh is progressive legislation, not divine self-correction. It is staged pedagogy — alcohol was banned in three steps — and each ruling was perfect for its time. Jewish and Christian scripture also supersedes earlier law, in the sacrificial system and in Acts 10. On the satanic verses, al-Albani in 'Nasb al-Majaniq' and others answer on the chains. Every chain of the story is broken, with no Companion eyewitness. It is absent from Bukhari and Muslim. It contradicts the Quran's own guarantee at 53:3-4. And its many mutually contradictory versions mark it as storyteller material. Scholars from Ibn Khuzaymah, who called it 'a fabrication of the heretics', to al-Albani have rejected it on transmission grounds.

responseSource.name: Al-Albani, 'Nasb al-Majaniq'; SeekersGuidance on naskh

rationale: Two components, two results. Abrogation as a phenomenon is conceded, since 2:106 is explicit and classical scholarship catalogued abrogated verses. Whether it is a defect is a theological judgment, and the progressive-legislation steelman is coherent. On the satanic-verses incident, Shahab Ahmed's demonstration of early universal acceptance is historically weighty, and 22:52 with 17:73-75 read most naturally as responses to a real event. title: Quran 4:34 on striking a wife, 4:24 on captives
claim: Quran 4:34 instructs that wives whose rebellion is feared be admonished, then abandoned in bed, then struck. claim: The biblical test of a prophet is verifiable prediction (Deuteronomy 18:21-22; Isaiah 41:21-23) and God-given signs (John 10:37-38). The Quran repeatedly records Muhammad declining to produce signs: 'Why has a sign not been sent down to him? Say: signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner' (29:50; also 13:7; 17:90-93; 6:37). Public miracles appear only in later hadith, which sits in tension with the Quran's own stance. The one claimed predictive prophecy is 30:2-4: 'The Romans have been defeated... but they will be victorious within three to nine years.' It is problematic on three counts. In the original undotted script the words could equally be read 'Rome has conquered... will be defeated'. The timespan is elastic. And on standard dating, from Jerusalem in 614 to final victory in 628, fulfilment falls outside nine years. A vague geopolitical reversal cannot meet Deuteronomy 18's standard of detailed, falsifiable prediction.

response: About Islam and Ibn Kathir answer on both points. The Rome prophecy was made when Byzantium lay prostrate, so predicting its victory was humanly absurd — and it happened, since Heraclius' improbable campaigns between 622 and 628 reversed the war. Abu Bakr's public wager (Jami at-Tirmidhi 3194) shows that 'Rome will win' was the reading from the start, and the recitation consensus fixes it. The same passage adds that the believers would rejoice at the same time, which was fulfilled at Badr. On signs, the Quran denies signs on demand to hostile testers, not miracles absolutely. The Quran's own inimitability, in the unanswered challenge of 2:23, is the standing miracle, and the splitting of the moon is referenced in 54:1-2 itself.

rationale: The Rome passage is a genuine pre-event prediction by any dating, so 'no prophecy at all' overstates the case, and Abu Bakr's wager is early evidence for the standard reading. But it survives as prophecy only in its vaguest form. The counter-reading in the defective script is real. The three-to-nine-year window fits only with favourable date choices. And one elastic reversal cannot bear the weight Deuteronomy 18 places on detailed, falsifiable prediction. Compare Isaiah naming Cyrus. The signs question is likewise split. The Quran's own posture, a warner without signs, is textually clear. It stands in real tension with the later hadith miracle corpus, which multiplies wonders the Quran never claims.

plain.d: Deuteronomy 18:21-22 gives a public test for a prophet. What he predicts must happen. Isaiah 41:21-23 sets the same standard for God himself. Jesus points to his works as evidence (John 10:37-38).

title: The aorta verse and the Khaybar poisoning
claim: Quran 69:44-46 says: 'If he had invented false sayings concerning Us, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta.' In Sahih al-Bukhari 4428, during his fatal illness, Muhammad says: 'O Aisha! I still feel the pain caused by the food I ate at Khaybar, and at this time I feel as if my aorta is being cut from that poison.' The poisoned meat was served by a Jewish woman after Khaybar's conquest, reportedly to test his prophethood, since she reasoned that a true prophet would be informed. The internal-test argument runs like this. The Quran names a specific divine punishment for a false prophet, a severed aorta. Islam's most authentic source records Muhammad dying while describing exactly that sensation, from a poisoning administered as a test of prophethood. His companion Bishr died of the same meal.

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 4428
Analyzing Islam — Poisoned at Khaybar; Aorta Severed (dossier)

response: IslamQA and Islamweb answer on the text. Quran 69:44-46 describes an immediate, public divine execution for forgery — seizure 'by the right hand' and instant severing, as a demonstration. It does not describe death by illness more than three years after a poisoning, since Khaybar was in 628 and the death in 632. 'I feel as if my aorta is being cut' is an Arabic idiom for mortal agony, using a different anatomical word — abhar rather than watin — so it is a simile of pain, not a report of the punishment in 69:46. Far from disproving him, the episode is claimed as vindication. The meat itself 'spoke' to warn him, he stopped eating, and death from its lingering effect earned him a martyr's honour, after the religion was completed (5:3). No forger controls his dying words, and attributing his death to the poison shows guileless candour.

responseSource.name: IslamQA and Islamweb treatments of Bukhari 4428 and 69:44-46

rationale: The factual chain is fully canonical. The verse, the poisoning as a test of prophethood, and the deathbed aorta statement are all in Bukhari. But the argument's force depends on reading 69:44-46 as a general criterion rather than as a threat of immediate exemplary execution. The Arabic uses different anatomical terms, and 'as if' marks a simile. The Christian can fairly say it is at minimum an astonishing irony that Islam's own canon has its prophet dying while describing the false prophet's punishment, poisoned in a test whose stated logic the outcome appeared to vindicate. The Muslim can fairly say the verse does not state the general criterion the argument needs. Powerful rhetoric; not a strict internal contradiction.

plain.d: Quran 69:44-46 says of the messenger: "If he had invented false sayings concerning Us, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta."

Sahih al-Bukhari 4428 records his final illness. He says to Aisha: "O Aisha! I still feel the pain caused by the food I ate at Khaybar, and at this time I feel as if my aorta is being cut from that poison." The poisoned meat was served by a Jewish woman after Khaybar fell. Reports say she did it to test his prophethood, reasoning that a true prophet would be warned. His companion Bishr died of the same meal.

plain.d: IslamQA and Islamweb answer on the text. Quran 69:44-46 describes an immediate, public execution for forgery — seizure by the right hand and instant severing, as a demonstration. It does not describe illness three years after a poisoning; Khaybar was 628 and he died in 632. The words are as if, a simile of mortal pain, and the anatomical terms differ — abhar in the hadith, watin in the verse. Muslims also read the episode as vindication: the meat warned him, he stopped eating, and dying from it earned him a martyr's honour after the religion was complete (5:3).

Every fact is canonical: the verse, the poisoning as a test, and the deathbed words are all in Islam's own books. The argument's force depends on reading 69:44-46 as a general rule rather than a threat of instant public punishment. That is where a Muslim can fairly push back.
Powerful rhetoric, not a strict contradiction. You can fairly call it an astonishing irony. You cannot fairly call it a proof. Say both halves, and let the other person weigh it.

title: Deeds on scales, no assurance even for Muhammad
claim: Islamic salvation is a weighing: 'Those whose scales are heavy — they are the successful; those whose scales are light — they have lost their souls, in Hell abiding' (23:102-103; 101:6-9; 7:8-9). Allah's love is conditional: 'Allah loves not the disbelievers' (3:32). Assurance is absent by design, even for Muhammad. 'By Allah, though I am Allah's Messenger, I neither know what will happen to me, nor to you' (Sahih al-Bukhari 7018, echoing Quran 46:9). And: 'none of you will enter Paradise by his deeds... not even I, unless Allah covers me with mercy' (Sahih Muslim 2816). The contrast is structural. The God of the Bible demonstrates love for sinners while they are still sinners (Romans 5:8). Salvation is by grace through faith and not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Sins are borne by a substitute (Isaiah 53:5-6). And assurance is offered as knowledge: 'that you may know that you have eternal life' (1 John 5:13).

response: The Yaqeen Institute's papers on salvation, and Ibn Qayyim on fear and hope, answer that Islam's soteriology is saturated with mercy rather than cold bookkeeping. Allah's mercy 'prevails over His wrath'. One good deed counts tenfold to seven-hundredfold, while a sin counts once (Sahih al-Bukhari 6491). Sincere monotheism ultimately delivers from eternal Hell, and Sahih Muslim 2816 shows that entry to Paradise is itself by Allah's mercy and not earned — which is functionally a doctrine of grace. The absence of presumptuous assurance is a feature, holding the believer between fear and hope, producing humility and moral seriousness, whereas guaranteed salvation invites licence; Christians themselves debate eternal security. Quran 3:32 concerns Allah's love of approval for persistent rejecters, not the absence of universal compassion (7:156). And Bukhari 7018 predates the revelation of Muhammad's forgiveness (48:1-2).

rationale: This entry documents a structural contrast, and every element of the Islamic side is canonical and conceded: salvation weighed by scales, no textual offer of assurance, conditional divine love in the Quran's explicit wording, and Muhammad's own recorded uncertainty. Note that 48:1-2 rescues Muhammad specifically, which underlines that others lack the guarantee. The steelman honestly complicates the caricature, since Muslim 2816 does place final entry on mercy. But mercy applied through a merit-weighing frame, with no substitutionary atonement and no offered assurance, remains categorically different from Romans 5:8 and 1 John 5:13. This is the entry that leads most directly to the gospel.

title: Taqiyya: hiding your faith under threat
claim: Islamic sources do allow deceit in set cases. Quran 16:106 excuses one who denies the faith under force. Quran 3:28 allows one to hide it from hostile unbelievers. The word there is tuqah, the root of taqiyya, which grew mainly in Shia law under attack. Sunni sources allow lying in three cases: war, making peace between people, and between spouses. That list is in Sahih Muslim 2605, where it comes through the narrator Ibn Shihab, and in Jami at-Tirmidhi 1939. Muhammad said 'war is deceit' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3030). Scripture runs the other way: God 'cannot lie' (Titus 1:2), and truth under threat is the martyr's calling (Matthew 10:28; Revelation 2:10). title: Sharia's death penalty for leaving Islam
claim: Classical Islamic law prescribes death for leaving Islam: 'Whoever changes his religion, kill him' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6922; compare 6878, which lists apostasy among the three grounds for lawful killing). All four Sunni schools carried the ruling, and it remains law in several states today. Quran 9:29 commands fighting the People of the Book 'until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled', establishing the dhimmi system of subordinated tolerance. Hudud punishments include amputation for theft (5:38) and stoning for adultery, from the sunnah (Sahih al-Bukhari 6829; Sahih Muslim 1690). The New Testament contrast is sharp. Faith is uncoerced — 'If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him' (John 12:47) — and the wheat and tares grow together till harvest (Matthew 13:29-30). The sword is renounced for the gospel's spread (Matthew 26:52; John 18:36). And apostates are to be won back, not executed (2 Timothy 2:24-26).

response: Reform-minded Muslim scholars argue from inside the tradition. 'No compulsion in religion' (2:256) is the Quran's own principle, and the Quran itself prescribes no worldly penalty for apostasy. The death penalty rests on hadith, and is best understood historically as punishing treason against the Muslim polity in wartime rather than private belief change — a view advanced by scholars such as Jonathan Brown and Taha Jabir Alalwani, and adopted by some modern states. Jizya was a tax in lieu of military service, often lighter than the zakat Muslims paid, and dhimmi status provided real protection that was unusual for its era. Hudud punishments carry near-impossible evidentiary standards, such as four eyewitnesses to the act, designed to make application rare — deterrence theatre more than practice.

title: Why 'Allah is a moon god' is false
claim: A popular claim in Christian counter-apologetics, popularised by Robert Morey's 'The Moon-God Allah' in 1994, holds that Allah was originally a pagan Arabian moon deity. It is often linked to the crescent symbol and to the South Arabian god Sin, or to Hubal. The conclusion drawn is that Muslims worship a repackaged idol. The argument circulates widely in tracts and online despite its evidentiary problems.

sources.name: Rick Brown, 'Who Is "Allah"?' (International Journal of Frontier Missions, 2006)
Islamic Awareness — reply to the 'Moon-God Allah' claim
Answering Islam — assessments cautioning against the Morey thesis

response: The rebuttal here is not a Muslim response but the evidence itself, acknowledged across the scholarly spectrum, including by Christian missiologists. 'Allah' is the ordinary Arabic word for God — the cognate of Hebrew Elohim and Aramaic Alaha. It was used by Arabic-speaking Jews and Christians before Islam, and it appears in every Arabic Bible to this day; Genesis 1:1 in Arabic begins 'In the beginning Allah created'. The Quran explicitly condemns worship of the moon: 'Do not prostrate to the sun or the moon' (41:37). The crescent symbol entered Islamic use centuries later, through the Ottomans. And Morey's archaeological linkages, including Hubal and the Sin temple at Hazor, are rejected by the relevant specialists.

title: Older Jewish and Christian tales in Allah's voice
claim: Several Quranic narratives track post-biblical Jewish and Christian legends rather than the Bible. Quran 5:32 — 'whoever kills a soul... it is as if he killed all mankind' — reproduces Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, a rabbinic homily on Cain composed centuries before Islam, and it even keeps the Israel-specific framing, 'We decreed upon the Children of Israel'. The preceding verse's raven, who shows Cain how to bury Abel (5:31), parallels the same midrashic cluster. Quran 18:9-26 retells the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, a Christian legend attested in Jacob of Serugh, who died in 521, and in Gregory of Tours, complete with the dog and the disputed head-count, presented as revelation about real 'youths of the cave'. Quran 21:68-69 has Abraham thrown into a fire, a story that arose from Genesis Rabbah's wordplay, reading 'Ur' of the Chaldees as ur, 'fire'. A book delivering eternal truth should not canonise identifiable human commentary, folklore and a pun as history.

Some alleged sources, such as Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer for the raven, may postdate Islam, which would reverse the direction of borrowing. And the Quran self-consciously corrects and reframes these accounts: on the Sleepers, 18:22 rebukes speculation about the number, which shows critical engagement rather than credulous copying. On 5:32, they argue that Allah confirming a truth he originally inspired to Israel's sages is no embarrassment, since the verse explicitly says the decree was given to the Children of Israel.

title: Seventy-two wives, or the presence of God
claim: The Quran's paradise is insistently sensual. There are wide-eyed maidens 'whom no man or jinn has touched' (55:56, 74), virgins made 'devoted, of equal age' for the companions of the right (56:35-38), 'full-breasted maidens of equal age' (78:33, kawa'ib atraban), along with wine, couches and served boys. The hadith intensify it. The martyr is 'married to seventy-two wives among the houris' (Jami at-Tirmidhi 1663, graded hasan sahih by Tirmidhi). Each man receives wives with marrow visible through their flesh, in a pearl tent sixty miles wide (Sahih al-Bukhari 3243). IslamQA 60188 affirms the houris as literal wives given for sexual enjoyment. Jesus taught the opposite: in the resurrection 'they neither marry nor are given in marriage' (Matthew 22:30), and heaven's centre is God himself dwelling with his people (Revelation 21:3; 22:4; Psalm 16:11). The contrast exposes what each faith holds as the ultimate good — reward, or God.

The number 72 comes from a single companion-chain that some scholars grade weaker, and renderings like 'full-breasted' for kawa'ib are contested. Believing wives, they note, are promised higher status than the houris.

title: Half a witness, half an heir under Islamic law
claim: Quran 2:282 requires two women to replace one male witness, 'so that if one errs, the other can remind her', and 4:11 fixes a daughter's inheritance at half a son's. Muhammad drew the theological conclusion himself: 'Is not the witness of a woman equal to half that of a man?... This is because of the deficiency of a woman's mind' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2658). In Sahih al-Bukhari 304 he declares women 'deficient in intelligence and religion' and 'the majority of the dwellers of Hell-fire'. These are not fringe readings. Classical fiqh built evidentiary and inheritance law on them, and they remain live in sharia codes today. Scripture's trajectory is different in kind. Male and female are jointly God's image (Genesis 1:27). The risen Christ's first commissioned witnesses were women (Luke 24:9-11), whose testimony was legally worthless in that culture and was preserved anyway. And in Christ 'there is no male and female' (Galatians 3:28).

response: IslamQA 111867 and classical commentators explain the 'deficiency' as domain-specific rather than essential. The testimony rule concerns financial contracts that women then rarely handled, so a second woman guards against error born of inexperience. The 'religion' deficiency refers only to exemption from prayer and fasting during menstruation, which is an excused lack and not a culpable one. Inheritance halves reflect economics, not worth, since men bear mandatory financial responsibility for women through the mahr and full family maintenance; a sister's unencumbered half can exceed a brother's encumbered whole. Modern Muslim scholars add that 2:282 is context-bound commercial procedure, and note other testimony contexts where a woman's word stands alone (24:6-9).

rationale: The texts and their operative legal force are undisputed; the defences reinterpret motive, not content. And the softening glosses collide with the sources themselves. Bukhari 2658 grounds the testimony rule in 'deficiency of mind', not in commercial inexperience, and the economics defence does not touch 'majority of the dwellers of Hell-fire'. Classical fiqh applied the half-witness rule far beyond finance, and states applying sharia apply it now. Because the substance is affirmed by Islam's most authentic hadith and by mainstream fatwa bodies, this is admitted. The honest debate is only over whether the arrangement is demeaning, which the texts' own stated rationale settles.

title: The Fatiha, seventeen times daily, on Jews and Christians
claim: Every observant Muslim recites Surah al-Fatiha in each unit of the five daily prayers, which is at minimum seventeen times daily. It closes with a plea to be guided in the path of those God favoured, 'not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who go astray' (1:7). Muhammad himself identified the referents: 'Those who have earned the anger are the Jews, and those who are led astray are the Christians' (Jami at-Tirmidhi 2954, graded hasan, from Adi ibn Hatim). Ibn Kathir records that 'the scholars of tafsir' held this view, citing broad early consensus, and it stands in Tafsir al-Jalalayn and in mainstream Salafi teaching today. So the world's second-largest religion liturgically defines itself, dozens of times a day, against Jews and Christians by name. Contrast the New Testament's posture toward those outside: 'love your enemies and pray for them' (Matthew 5:44), and Paul's 'my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved' (Romans 10:1).

title: Islam's whole memory of Muhammad rests on hadith
claim: Almost all that Islam knows of Muhammad comes from hadith. They were first written down long after his death in 632. That includes how to pray, the five pillars, the age of Aisha, the events of his life, and even the story of how the Quran was gathered. Al-Bukhari died in 870. He is said to have sifted some 600,000 reports in circulation and kept about 7,000, counting repeats. So the Muslim community itself made up false reports on a vast scale for two centuries. Western scholars pressed the point. Ignaz Goldziher, Joseph Schacht and G. H. A. Juynboll showed that chains were improved and pushed back in time, and that 'common links' point to chains made up whole. The trap for dawah is simple. If the hadith cannot be trusted, Islam cannot say its own prayers, fix its pillars, or tell its prophet's life, and the Quran floats free of context. If they can be trusted, then Bukhari's hard reports stand too: Aisha at nine, the spell, Banu Qurayza, and 'deficient in mind'. The Gospels, by contrast, were written while eyewitnesses lived, a fraction of that gap.

Early written notes, such as the sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih, push the paper trail back near the first generation. Motzki's method, which reads chain and text together, verifies material Schacht threw out. Jonathan Brown notes that the tradition catalogued false reports itself, with a care Western critics only later found. And the 600,000 figure counts chain-variants, not separate lies.

title: Surah 66: an oath dissolved by revelation
claim: Surah 66 opens with Allah rebuking Muhammad: 'O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives?' (66:1). It then dissolves his oath (66:2) and warns his wives that if he divorces them Allah will give him better ones (66:5). Sunan an-Nasa'i 3959, graded sahih by al-Albani, supplies the occasion. Muhammad 'had intercourse with' his slave woman, identified in tafsir as Mariya the Copt, in Hafsa's quarters or on her day. Aisha and Hafsa pressed him until he swore Mariya forbidden to himself, whereupon revelation descended freeing him from the oath. An alternative sahih occasion, in Sahih al-Bukhari 4912, involves only honey. Either way the shape matches the Zaynab pattern this site already covers. Heaven steps in, promptly and exactly, to release Muhammad from a bind at home. That is precisely what Aisha noted dryly: 'your Lord hastens to fulfill your wishes'.

The Mariya narrations, they argue, are aberrant, or shadhdh, or later conflated accounts. And even if some chain is technically sound, occasion-of-revelation reports are notoriously fluid. On the substance, the surah shows Muhammad's humanity and Allah's correction — he is rebuked, not indulged. And the principle established, that one may not make the lawful unlawful by oath, is sober jurisprudence, with expiation prescribed (66:2), matching Quran 5:89.

Combined with 33:37 and 33:50-51, already in this app, it exhibits revelation repeatedly bending toward the prophet's personal convenience. title: Mut'ah: temporary marriage, permitted then banned
claim: Sahih hadith establish that Muhammad permitted mut'ah, a marriage contracted for a fixed term and payment that dissolves automatically. Companions on campaign were allowed to marry women 'for a fixed time', even for a garment (Sahih Muslim 1404), and Jabir reports that the practice continued through Abu Bakr's reign until Umar banned it (Sahih Muslim 1405). Sunni Islam holds that Muhammad finally prohibited it (Sahih al-Bukhari 5115; Sahih Muslim 1406, 'Allah has forbidden it until the Day of Resurrection'), though the abrogation is variously dated to Khaybar, to the conquest of Mecca, or to Umar's caliphate. Shia Islam rejects the abrogation, grounds the practice in Quran 4:24 — 'give them their due compensation for what you have enjoyed' — and practises mut'ah today, where in documented cases it functions as religiously laundered prostitution. Either Muhammad sanctioned term-limited sexual contracts, or the community that transmitted his religion cannot agree on what he finally commanded. Both horns matter against 'a marriage covenant witnessed by God' (Malachi 2:14).

title: The Black Stone and rites older than Islam
claim: Islam's central rites predate Islam. The Kaaba was a functioning pagan shrine housing 360 idols until Muhammad cleansed it in 630 (Sahih al-Bukhari 4287). Had I not seen the Prophet kissing you, I would not have kissed you' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1597). Other hadith give the stone unusual powers. It came down from paradise whiter than milk. Sins turned it black. It will testify on judgment day (Jami at-Tirmidhi 877, 961). So there is a question for a faith that defines itself against idols. title: Surah 9, the sword verses, and what came last
claim: Surah 9, by Muslim consensus among the last revealed, commands 'kill the polytheists wherever you find them' after the sacred months (9:5), and 'fight those who do not believe in Allah... from the People of the Book until they pay the jizya with willing submission, and feel themselves subdued' (9:29). Ibn Kathir's tafsir records Ad-Dahhak's judgment that the Verse of the Sword 'abrogated every agreement of peace between the Prophet and any idolator, every treaty, and every term'. Classical jurists across the schools built offensive-jihad doctrine on exactly this chronology, and Muhammad's own summary is canonical: 'I have been ordered to fight the people until they say: none has the right to be worshipped but Allah' (Sahih al-Bukhari 25). The frequently quoted 'no compulsion in religion' (2:256) is Medinan but earlier, which is why the classical tradition, not Islamophobes, treated the sword verses as operative. title: Bukhari's report of a spell cast on Muhammad
claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 3268, narrated by Aisha, reports that a Jewish sorcerer, Labid ibn al-A'sam, worked magic on Muhammad using his hair and a comb, 'so that he began to imagine that he had done a thing which he had not really done'. By some accounts the state lasted months. Sahih Muslim 2189 carries the same account, so it is as authenticated as hadith get. The problem is double. Internally, the Quran indignantly denies the charge that Muhammad was 'a bewitched man' (17:47; 25:8), yet Islam's most authentic hadith affirm exactly that. And there is a deeper problem about knowledge. A prophet whose mind could be made to experience things that never happened, by a hostile magician, for an extended period during his revelatory career, has no way to certify which of his experiences were genuine. The biblical test excludes this outright, since God's true prophet is not overpowered by sorcery — 'there is no enchantment against Jacob' (Numbers 23:23) — and God's word does not come through a compromised channel (Deuteronomy 18:21-22).

It was an illness like any bodily ailment prophets suffer. It ended in a miracle, since Allah revealed the spell's location and cure, as the hadith itself reports, with Surahs 113 and 114 linked to the deliverance. And 25:8's denial concerns the pagans' charge that the Quran itself was the product of sorcery, which is a different claim from the prophet suffering a temporary spell. Some early scholars and modernists simply rejected the report as contradicting the Quran.

The hadith's own description — believing he had done what he had not done — is a defect of perception and memory, the exact faculties revelation depends on. No criterion is offered by which Muhammad or anyone else could separate bewitched experiences from genuine ones. And the minority who reject the report to save the Quran, which is a live Muslim position, impale themselves on the hadith-epistemology dilemma. Bukhari's most rigorously authenticated Aisha material would fall, and Islamic method would fall with it. The internal tension with 25:8 is answered only by redescribing the pagans' charge. No resolution holds all three: sahih hadith, Quranic denial, and prophetic reliability.

plain.d: Sahih al-Bukhari 3268 carries a report from Aisha. A Jewish man named Labid ibn al-A'sam worked magic on Muhammad, using his hair and a comb. The effect was that "he began to imagine that he had done a thing which he had not really done." Some accounts say it lasted months. Sahih Muslim 2189 has the same account.
The Quran rejects the charge with heat. Quran 17:47 and 25:8 say the wrongdoers call him a bewitched man. Yet Islam's most trusted hadith say a spell was cast on him.

A mind can be made to hold things that never happened. That is what the report says was done to him. If it can happen for months, during the years of revelation, how would he know which experiences were real? The Bible rules this out for a prophet. "There is no enchantment against Jacob" (Numbers 23:23).

And those who reject the report to save the Quran fall into the hadith problem instead. Bukhari's best Aisha material would go, and the method with it.

title: Ezra as God's son, a claim no Jew made
claim: Quran 9:30 asserts as fact: 'The Jews say: Ezra (Uzair) is the son of Allah.' It is set in parallel with the Christian confession of Christ, and Allah's curse is pronounced on both groups for it. But no Jewish text, sect or tradition in the entire historical record calls Ezra the son of God. Not the Tanakh, the Talmud, the Mishnah, Philo, Josephus, Qumran, or any rabbinic source. Judaism's defining confession is the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), and deifying a scribe would be its ultimate blasphemy. Historians call the verse enigmatic precisely because the belief is unattested. The error matters doubly for dawah. An omniscient author does not misreport the theology of a community living in Medina alongside Muhammad. title: Why 'Allah is a foreign god's name' fails
claim: A popular evangelical polemic claims that 'Allah' is intrinsically the name of a false deity, so Muslims linguistically worship someone other than the biblical God, and Christians must never use the word. title: A cave, terror, and the Christian who explained it
claim: By Islam's own most trusted sources, Muhammad's first encounter with revelation left him terrified and unable to identify its source. title: Quran 2:62 and 3:85 on who is saved
claim: Quran 2:62 promises that 'those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians — whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteousness — will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them'. Quran 5:69 repeats the promise nearly verbatim. Yet Quran 3:85 declares: 'Whoever desires other than Islam as religion — never will it be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers' (compare 3:19). The classical resolution concedes the tension. Al-Tabari's tafsir on 2:62 records Ibn Abbas saying the verse was abrogated by 3:85, though Mujahid and al-Dahhak held 2:62 muhkama, still standing, and al-Tabari himself preferred a restricted reading. Sahih Muslim 153 seals the exclusivist position, since any Jew or Christian who hears of Muhammad and dies without believing his message 'will be among the inhabitants of the Fire'. Modern scholars split between abrogation and restriction. Either way the two texts pull in opposite directions, and the abrogation solution is itself an admission of it.

title: Slavery regulated in Islamic law, ended from outside

title: Female circumcision, a disputed hadith in classical law

title: Grammatical oddities in a book claiming perfect Arabic
claim: The Quran rests its great miracle on language nobody can match — 'produce a surah like it' (2:23) — in 'clear Arabic' (12:2). Yet classical scholars themselves listed odd forms. Arabic marks case by word endings. Quran 4:162 has al-muqimina, 'those who establish prayer', in one case while the nouns around it stand in another. Quran 5:69 has al-sabi'una in a form the particle inna should not allow, unlike 2:62 and 22:17, where the same word follows the rule. Quran 20:63 reads inna hadhani la-sahirani, where inna calls for hadhayni. Quran 2:177 does the same with al-sabirina. Early reports admit the problem. Uthman is said to have remarked of the compiled text, 'I see errors (lahn) in it, and the Arabs will correct them with their tongues.' And a report through Abu Ubayd's Fada'il al-Qur'an has Aisha judge that 4:162, 5:69 and 20:63 are 'the fault of the scribes'. Both reports are themselves disputed, since their chains are contested and Muslim scholars reject or reread them. Classical grammarians smoothed each verse by appeal to poetic licence, dialect and the praise form — which is itself a sign that the oddities were felt.

response: Muslim grammarians and modern academics, including Islamic Awareness, answer that these are attested classical Arabic and not errors. The form in 4:162 and 2:177 is the well-known qat' construction, used for praise, meaning 'and especially those who...', and it appears in pre-Islamic poetry. The form in 5:69 can be a delayed topic. And 20:63's hadhani matches the speech of certain Arab tribes, said to be Banu al-Harith, who keep the same dual form in every case. The earliest word scholars knew that reading. The Uthman and Aisha reports, they argue, are unreliable. Their chains are contested. Lahn in early usage could mean a style of reciting rather than an error. And it is hard to believe Uthman would standardise a text he thought faulty, while companions who had memorised it raised no objection. Grammar books were written after the Quran, and partly from it.

title: Quran 65:4 and wives 'who have not yet menstruated'
claim: Quran 65:4 legislates the iddah, the waiting period after divorce, for three groups of wives, including those 'who have not menstruated'. The classical commentators — al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and the standard tafsir tradition — uniformly read this as girls who have not yet reached puberty. Since Quran 33:49 says no iddah exists at all for an unconsummated marriage, the verse presupposes consummated marriages to prepubescent girls. That embeds child marriage in the Quran's own divorce legislation, independently of the Aisha biography.

response: Modern apologists, such as Discover The Truth, argue that 'those who have not menstruated' refers to adult women with delayed menarche or amenorrhea, not to children. They add that the verse addresses waiting periods generally without endorsing child marriage, and some note that a marriage contract does not imply consummation. This stands in contrast with the classical position in Ibn Kathir and in Ma'arif al-Qur'an, which state that the verse covers 'the young who have not reached the years of menstruation'.

The tafsir tradition is unanimous that the clause covers the not-yet-pubescent, and the fiqh manuals of all four schools drew the corresponding rule. The iddah logic is the trap. Quran 33:49 removes any waiting period for unconsummated marriages, so an iddah for the never-menstruated only has work to do if such marriages were consummated. This is the legislative twin of the Aisha case. Even if every biographical report were discarded, the law would remain in the text.

title: Four witnesses, or eighty lashes for the accuser
claim: Quran 24:4 requires four eyewitnesses to prove unlawful intercourse. An accuser who cannot produce them receives eighty lashes, and 24:13 applies the same test. Classical fiqh placed rape, zina-bil-jabr, under the rules of proof for zina. Pakistan wrote that into the 1979 Hudood Ordinance. The result is documented. Women who reported rape were prosecuted for zina, their complaint read as an admission of intercourse they could not prove was forced. It took secular law, the Women's Protection Act of 2006, to move rape out of that framework and back into the Penal Code.

They add that rape could alternatively be prosecuted as hiraba, violent crime, without four witnesses. And they argue that the Hudood Ordinance was bad man-made legislation rather than true sharia — as shown by the Pakistani religious scholars who supported the 2006 reform. Both the reformist and traditional positions are surveyed in the Washington and Lee Law Review article on twenty-five years of the Hudood Ordinances and in the 2006 reform debate.

The instructive contrast is Deuteronomy 22:25-27, which explicitly declares the rape victim innocent — 'to the young woman you shall do nothing' — with no witness quota imposed on her. As a usage note, lead with the Pakistan history, which is documented, and acknowledge 24:4's anti-slander context up front. It makes the argument stronger, not weaker.

title: Satan among the angels, or one of the jinn
claim: Five times the Quran says the angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam, 'and they prostrated, except Iblis' (2:34; 7:11; 15:30-31; 20:116; 38:73-74). That is grammar which counts Iblis among the angels. But 18:50 says 'he was of the jinn, so he rebelled'. The Quran also says angels never disobey Allah (66:6), yet on the angel reading Iblis did exactly that. And Iblis says he was created from fire (7:12), while the hadith says angels were created from light and jinn from smokeless fire (Sahih Muslim 2996).

response: The tafsir literature offers three classical harmonisations. Al-Tabari, following reports from Ibn Abbas, holds that Iblis belonged to a tribe of angels called 'jinn', guardians of Paradise, created from fire. Al-Hasan al-Basri, cited approvingly by Ibn Kathir, holds that Iblis 'was not an angel for the twinkling of an eye', and that the exception in 2:34 is a disconnected exception, meaning he was merely among the angels when the command came. Al-Baydawi holds that he was created an angel and became jinn by his deed.

Al-Hasan al-Basri's 'never an angel' saves 18:50, but only by making the Quran's own repeated sentence structure misleading five times over. In conversation this is a clean, self-contained internal-consistency test that requires no external sources, only the Quran read carefully. Pick either horn and let the tafsir tradition supply the contradiction.

title: Six days of creation, and Surah 41's arithmetic
claim: Four passages say the heavens and earth were created in six days: 7:54, 10:3, 11:7 and 25:59. But 41:9-12 itemises the stages. The earth took two days. Then, thumma, mountains and provisions took four days. Then, thumma, the seven heavens took two days. Two plus four plus two is eight. There is a bonus tension as well. In 41:9-12 the earth is completed before the heavens, while 79:27-30 builds the heaven first and spreads the earth 'after that', ba'da dhalika.

Nobody reads 'I built the house in two days, then finished the roof in four days' as six days total, except by special pleading. Translators sympathetic to the harmonisation must insert parenthetical glosses, such as 'four days including the former two', that are not in the Arabic. Note honestly if it is raised that Christians read Genesis's days in more than one way too. But Genesis's numbers at least add up.

plain.t: The Muslim answer, at full strength
plain.d: IslamQA 31865, following Ibn Kathir, gives the standard reply. The four days of 41:10 are inclusive. The earth took two days, and its mountains and provisions took two more, so four means four in total up to that point. Four plus two is six.

Genuinely arguable, and small. The inclusive reading has to fight the word thumma, which marks sequence in Arabic. Translators who favour the harmony insert glosses that are not in the Arabic. Be honest if it comes up: Christians read the days of Genesis in more than one way too. Genesis simply does not have this arithmetic problem.
"Two, then four, then two. How do you get six out of that? I would like to understand it."

title: Qadar: 'created for Hell' before they are born
claim: The Quran teaches that Allah decrees everything, including belief and disbelief. 'We have created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind' (7:179). 'Whomever Allah leaves astray, none can guide' (7:178). 'Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us' (9:51). 'You do not will unless Allah wills' (76:30; 81:29). In Sahih al-Bukhari 6594 the angel writes each person's deeds, and whether he is 'doomed or blessed', before birth. Sahih al-Bukhari 6596 is titled 'The pen has dried'. So Allah creates people for Hell and then punishes them for what he decreed.

rationale: Kasb re-labels the problem rather than solving it. Muslim scholars themselves proverbially listed al-Ash'ari's kasb among the famously unintelligible doctrines. And the Quran's language is stronger than mere foreknowledge: created for Hell (7:179), 'I will surely fill Hell' (32:13), and Allah 'sends astray whom He wills' (14:4). The biblical contrast is the point for conversation. The God of Scripture 'takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked' (Ezekiel 33:11; compare 18:23), 'desires all people to be saved' (1 Timothy 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9), and pleads 'choose life' (Deuteronomy 30:19). The answer is that no Christian tradition teaches that God delights in damnation, or creates men in order to damn them.

title: Triple talaq: to remarry, she must marry another
claim: Quran 2:230 says that after a third divorce a woman is not lawful to her husband again 'until she has married another husband'. Muhammad applied it literally. When Rifa'a's thrice-divorced wife wanted to return to him, he answered, 'No — not until he tastes your sweetness and you taste his sweetness' (Sahih al-Bukhari 5260), meaning the intervening marriage must be consummated. The rule generated halala, or tahleel — arranged one-night marriages to re-legalise a wife — a practice still sold as a service today. And instant triple talaq remained live law until Muslim-majority jurisdictions legislated against it. In India it was struck down in Shayara Bano in 2017 and criminalised in 2019.

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 5260
