response: Muslims respond on three fronts. First, a contracted halala — marrying with the prior intention of divorcing in order to re-legalise the woman — is itself cursed and invalid in the hadith, since the muhallil, 'the one who makes lawful', is condemned; see IslamQA 159041. Second, the rule in 2:230 is a deterrent, designed to make men take divorce seriously. Third, instant triple talaq in one sitting, talaq-e-biddat, is a condemned innovation and not original Islam.

responseSource.name: IslamQA 159041; mainstream Sunni fiqh on tahleel

rationale: The curse on the muhallil only forbids the arrangement being explicit. The underlying rule stands on any reading. A thrice-divorced woman cannot return to her husband until another man has consummated a marriage with her, and Sahih al-Bukhari 5260 puts the consummation requirement in Muhammad's own mouth. The 'deterrent' framing concedes the mechanism, since the deterrent's payload is the wife's sexual union with another man. The clandestine halala-service market, documented by the BBC in the UK and litigated in India, is the rule's predictable equilibrium. And it took a secular constitutional court, over the opposition of the All India Muslim Personal Law Board, to kill the trigger practice. Contrast Jesus: divorce concessions exist 'because of your hardness of heart' (Matthew 19:8-9), with no ritual requiring the woman's body as the price of reconciliation.

plain.d: A husband may divorce by pronouncement. After the third one it is final. Quran 2:230 then says the woman is not lawful to him again "until she has married another husband."

Rifa'a's thrice-divorced wife wanted to return to him. The answer was: "No — not until he tastes your sweetness and you taste his sweetness" (Sahih al-Bukhari 5260). That means the marriage in between must be consummated.

Halala, also called tahleel. It is an arranged marriage for one night, so a couple can remarry. It is still sold as a service today, documented by the BBC in the UK. Instant triple talaq stayed live law until courts acted. India struck it down in Shayara Bano in 2017 and made it a crime in 2019.

plain.t: The Muslim answer, at full strength
plain.d: IslamQA 159041 answers on three fronts. An arranged halala is itself cursed and invalid, since the hadith condemn the muhallil, the man who makes her lawful. The rule in 2:230 is a deterrent, meant to make men take divorce seriously. And instant triple talaq in one sitting, talaq-e-biddat, is a condemned innovation rather than original Islam.

They admit the rule itself. The curse only forbids saying the plan out loud. Underneath, a thrice-divorced woman still cannot return until another man has consummated a marriage with her, and Bukhari 5260 puts that in Muhammad's own mouth. The deterrent framing concedes the mechanism, since the deterrent's payload is her body. And it took a secular court, against the All India Muslim Personal Law Board, to end the trigger. Compare Jesus: divorce was allowed for hardness of heart, with no ritual requiring a woman's body as the price of reconciliation.
"Why should a woman have to sleep with another man before her husband can take her back?"

title: Surah 9 opens without 'in the name of God'
claim: Surah 9, al-Tawbah or Bara'ah, is the only one of 114 surahs lacking the bismillah heading. Asked why, Uthman explained in Jami at-Tirmidhi 3086 that al-Anfal came early in Medina and Bara'ah late, that its subject matter resembled al-Anfal's, and that the Prophet died without clarifying whether it was part of it. 'So I put them adjacent and did not write the basmala between them.' The caliph who standardised the Quran describes a surah boundary settled by his own inference, not by revelation.

sources.name: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3086
IslamQA 173672 — 'Why There Is No Bismillah in Surah At-Tawbah'
Abu Amina Elias — why bismillah is missing from Surat al-Tawbah

response: The common devotional answer, surveyed at IslamQA 173672, is that the basmala, which is the mercy formula, was deliberately omitted because al-Tawbah opens with a declaration of war and the repudiation of treaties. A surah of the sword needs no invocation of mercy, a view attributed to Ali. Others hold that the surah order and boundaries were fixed by the Prophet's instruction, tawqifi. And Uthman's account is graded variously, with Darussalam calling it hasan while some later critics weaken it.

responseSource.name: IslamQA 173672 and classical opinions surveyed there

rationale: The two traditional answers undercut each other. If the omission were a revealed judgment about mercy and war, Uthman would not have explained it as his own uncertainty about where one surah ends and another begins. State the weakness plainly: the grading of Tirmidhi 3086 is contested, so use this as corroboration inside the compilation story rather than as your lead. This site's uthman-burning and compilation cases carry the primary weight. The undisputed core is untouched by the grading dispute. The basmala is missing, the companion codices ordered surahs differently, and the arrangement of the mushaf passed through editorial decisions made after Muhammad.

plain.d: Each chapter of the Quran opens the same way. It begins with the basmala: in the name of God, the Merciful, the Kind. One chapter does not. Surah 9 has no such line.

He was asked why. His answer is in Jami at-Tirmidhi 3086. Surah 8 came early in Medina. Surah 9 came late. The two were alike in theme. The Prophet died and never said if they were one chapter or two. "So I put them adjacent and did not write the basmala between them." The man who fixed the text is telling us he made a call.

plain.t: The Muslim answer, at full strength
plain.d: IslamQA 173672 gives the common answer. The line was left out on purpose. Surah 9 opens with war and the ending of treaties. A chapter of the sword needs no call for mercy. That view is traced to Ali. Others say the order of the chapters was set by the Prophet himself, which they call tawqifi. And the grading of Tirmidhi 3086 is in dispute. Darussalam calls it hasan. Some later critics call it weak.

Genuinely arguable, and do not lead with it. The two answers cut against each other. If God had left the line out to mark a book of war, Uthman would not have said he was unsure where one chapter ended. But the grading fight is real. So use this to back up the wider story, not to open. The core is safe either way. The line is missing. Other copies had the chapters in a different order. And a man set the shape of the book after the Prophet died.
"Uthman said he made the call himself. What do you make of that?"

refwhy.Jami at-Tirmidhi 3086: From Tirmidhi, not one of the two Sahih books, and its grade is disputed. It holds Uthman's own account.

title: Haman in Egypt, a thousand years too early
claim: The Quran places a figure named Haman in Egypt as Pharaoh's officer at the time of Moses (28:6; 28:8; 28:38; 29:39; 40:24; 40:36-37). Pharaoh even asks Haman to fire bricks and build a lofty tower, so as to look upon the God of Moses. But Haman is the vizier of the Persian king in the book of Esther (3:1), set roughly a millennium after Moses. And the tower-to-heaven motif belongs to Babel (Genesis 11:3-4), where baked bricks are likewise specified. The Quran reads like a fusion of Esther's villain with the Babel story, relocated to Egypt — exactly the blend already circulating in Jewish midrashic storytelling.

sources.name: Adam J. Silverstein, 'Haman' (Princeton University Press)
Silverstein, 'Haman in the Qur'an' — chapter in 'Veiling Esther, Unveiling Her Story' (Oxford)

response: Two Muslim defences are offered. The first is that the Quranic Haman is simply a different Egyptian with a similar name. The second is the 'scientific miracle' version, popularised from Maurice Bucaille and developed by Islamic Awareness. The letters hmn-h appear in an Egyptian name catalogue, as a chief of stone-quarry workers, so on this reading the Quran preserves an authentic Egyptian name that history had lost.

responseSource.name: Islamic Awareness, following Bucaille

rationale: The hmn-h argument dissolves on inspection. It rests on reading a German-transliterated entry in a name lexicon. The reconstructed vowels are conjectural. No Egyptologist endorses 'Haman' as an Egyptian name. And the alleged quarry chief has no connection to Moses's era, or to a vizier's role. Meanwhile the academic treatment, by Adam J. Silverstein and published by Princeton and Oxford, concludes that both Hamans are the same folkloric villain, migrating between the Persian and Pharaonic courts through the fluidity of Near Eastern narrative. Silverstein is no Christian apologist. That frame concedes precisely what the dictation-from-heaven model cannot afford: the Quran inherited a literary character, complete with Babel's bricks and tower, and set him in the wrong court. It pairs naturally with this site's Samaritan-anachronism and Dhul-Qarnayn cases, as a third independent instance of the same pattern.

Haman is the vizier of the Persian king in the book of Esther (Esther 3:1). That is roughly a thousand years after Moses. And the tower-to-heaven with baked bricks belongs to Babel (Genesis 11:3-4).
It reads as Esther's villain joined to the Babel story and moved to Egypt. That blend was already told in Jewish story-telling.

That concedes the decisive point: the Quran inherited a literary character, bricks and tower included, and set him in the wrong court.
"Haman is the villain of Esther, in Persia, a thousand years later. Would you read the two accounts with me?"

title: The fly-wing hadith and the miracle-of-science claim
claim: Dawah routinely claims that Muhammad's words anticipate modern science. The sahih medical corpus is the test. Dip the fly in your drink, because one wing carries the disease and the other its cure (Sahih al-Bukhari 3320). The tribesmen of Ukl and Urayna were prescribed camel milk and camel urine as medicine (Sahih al-Bukhari 233; 5686). And black seed is 'a healing for every disease except death' (Sahih al-Bukhari 5688). A source reliable enough to establish embryology miracles is reliable enough to own these.

The vindication studies are small, in fringe journals, and post hoc — and the WHO warns against consuming camel urine, which was a live issue during MERS. And once 'every disease except death' is hyperbole, the method that finds precise embryology in equally loose language collapses. As a usage note, deploy this as a response when the scientific-miracles claim is made. As a cold-open attack it reads as mockery and closes the conversation.

title: Adam at ninety feet, and people shrinking since
claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 3326 says: 'Allah created Adam, making him 60 cubits tall', which is roughly 27 to 30 metres, or 90 feet. It ends: 'people have been decreasing in stature since Adam's creation'. Sahih al-Bukhari 6227 and Sahih Muslim 2841 carry the report as well. Both clauses are empirically testable and false. No giant human remains exist, and the skeletal record runs the other way, since average stature has increased in recent centuries and no ancient population approached even three metres.

Notably, Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani had already flagged the problem in Fath al-Bari in the 15th century. He observed that the dwellings and remains of ancient nations do not indicate such heights, and confessed difficulty resolving it.

That reframes every 'but it's sahih' appeal elsewhere, including on Aisha's age, the fly, and the sun's prostration. Keep it as a supporting case, not a lead.

title: Muslim scholarship rejects the 'Aisha was 19' rescue
claim: A popular modern Muslim counter to the Aisha case runs as follows. The age-nine report comes from a single narrator, Hisham ibn Urwa, whose memory failed in Iraq. And calculations from his sister Asma's age — ten years older, and dead at 100 in 73 AH — put Aisha at 17 to 19 at consummation.

The Yaqeen Institute and ICRAA, both mainstream Muslim institutions, defend age nine and label the 19 thesis methodological revisionism.
